families.s: HSE workplace fresh-air and ventilation assessment guidance
families.t: fresh-air duty, natural and mechanical ventilation, poor-air identification, system operation, maintenance and worker consultation
f: Employers must ensure every enclosed workplace is ventilated by a sufficient quantity of fresh or purified air.
Ventilation brings fresh air into a workplace and removes stale, hot, humid or polluted indoor air.
Poorly ventilated areas should be identified by considering occupancy, room use, openings and the performance of mechanical systems.
Natural ventilation can be increased by opening suitable windows, doors and vents without compromising fire precautions.
Mechanical recirculation systems should include and operate fresh-air inlets where required to avoid unhealthy air.
Natural, mechanical or mixed ventilation may be appropriate depending on the building and workplace activity.
Carbon-dioxide monitoring can support assessment in occupied spaces but does not directly measure all pollutants or prove ventilation adequacy by itself.
Ventilation arrangements should be maintained, reviewed and discussed with workers when conditions or occupancy change.
families.g: Ventilation adequacy depends on room volume, occupancy, activity, outdoor-air supply, distribution, system condition, pollutants, weather and how the space is actually used.

families.s: HSE general workplace welfare and facility guidance
families.t: toilets, washing, drinking water, clothing storage, rest and eating areas, cleanliness, room, seating, temperature and safe premises
f: Workers must have access to toilets and hand-washing facilities with soap and a means of drying hands.
Employers must provide wholesome drinking water.
Workers need suitable places to store clothing and to change when special work clothing is required.
A suitable place must be available for workers to rest and eat meals.
A healthy workplace requires adequate ventilation, reasonable temperature and lighting suitable for the work.
Workplaces should provide enough room, suitable workstations and appropriate seating.
Premises and equipment must be maintained, floors and routes kept clear, and suitable waste containers provided.
The number and type of toilets and washing facilities should reflect the workforce and be kept clean, ventilated, lit and supplied.
families.g: Required welfare provision depends on workforce size and composition, shift pattern, work type, contamination, mobility, accessibility needs and the location and duration of work.

families.s: HSE workplace safety-sign and signal guidance
families.t: sign necessity, risk-control hierarchy, traffic signs, maintenance, worker instruction, colour and signal meaning
f: Employers must provide safety signs where a significant risk remains that cannot be avoided or adequately controlled by other means.
A sign is unnecessary where it would not help reduce risk or the risk is not significant.
Road-traffic signs should be used where necessary to regulate vehicle movement in workplaces.
Provided safety signs must be maintained so that they remain visible and effective.
Workers must be told the meaning of unfamiliar signs and the action required when they see them.
The Safety Signs and Signals Regulations cover signs, hand signals, acoustic signals and illuminated signals used for health and safety.
Signs supplement rather than replace engineering controls, safe systems of work, supervision and training.
Sign selection and positioning should make the message clear to the people exposed without creating confusion or excessive competing warnings.
families.g: Sign effectiveness depends on the remaining hazard, visibility, lighting, language and familiarity, placement, maintenance, competing information and the actions workers can actually take.

families.t: natural and artificial light, shadow control, colour recognition, task lighting, emergency routes and lighting failure
f: Construction areas in use should be arranged to use natural light where reasonably practicable.
Artificial lighting is required where natural light is inadequate or work continues outside daylight hours.
Lighting must not distort the apparent colour or visibility of safety signs and safety-critical equipment.
Additional lighting may be needed where shadows obscure tools, edges, stairwells or other hazards.
Emergency lighting is required where failure of primary lighting would create a health or safety risk.
Emergency escape routes should remain adequately lit while workers are present.
Emergency lighting need only provide enough illumination for safe escape rather than normal production work.
Lighting design should consider illuminance, glare, contrast, flicker, shadows, maintenance and the visual demands of the task.
families.g: Lighting risk depends on task detail, layout, contrast, glare, shadows, weather, time, lamp condition, emergency arrangements and the visual capability of workers.

families.s: HSE safe ladder and stepladder selection and use guidance
families.t: low-risk short-duration use, pre-use checks, stability, securing, angle, climbing, loading, positioning and overhead hazards
f: Ladders are appropriate only where a risk assessment shows that more protective equipment is not justified for low-risk, short-duration work.
The ladder must be suitable, in good condition, checked before use and used by a competent person.
A leaning ladder should normally be positioned using the one-in-four rule, approximately a 75-degree angle.
The user should face the ladder and maintain a secure handhold while climbing or descending.
Leaning ladders should be level, stable and secured where reasonably practicable.
Users should avoid overreaching, overloading and working from prohibited top steps or rungs.
Ladders must not be placed on movable objects or used as improvised extensions to other access equipment.
Work near overhead electrical lines requires separate controls and safe clearance or isolation.
families.g: Ladder suitability depends on height, duration, task force, ground, securing points, traffic, weather, electrical hazards, carried materials, user capability and available alternatives.

families.s: HSE general scaffold design, erection, inspection and access-security guidance
families.t: design, competence, foundations, ties, platforms, guardrails, loading, inspection, modification and unauthorised access
f: Scaffolds must be designed, erected, altered and dismantled by competent people under competent supervision.
Scaffold foundations, standards, ledgers, bracing and ties must provide adequate strength and stability.
Working platforms require suitable decking, guardrails, intermediate protection, toe boards and safe access.
Scaffold loads must remain within the design and component limits.
Scaffolds must be inspected after installation, at prescribed intervals and after events that could affect safety.
Unsafe scaffolds should not be used until defects are corrected.
Unauthorised access should be prevented using site security, ladder removal or suitable ladder guards where necessary.
Modification or removal of ties and components should occur only under an approved design and controlled system.
families.g: Scaffold safety depends on design class, height, loading, foundations, ties, sheeting, weather, erection sequence, inspections, alterations, access and adjacent public or traffic risks.

families.s: HSE mobile tower-scaffold erection, stability, inspection and movement guidance
families.t: competent assembly, manufacturer instructions, outriggers, guardrails, inspection, wind, movement and misuse prevention
f: The selected tower must be suitable for the work and erected and dismantled by trained, competent people.
The manufacturer or supplier instructions must define the erection sequence, bracing and safe maximum height.
Towers should stand on firm level ground with castors locked or base plates correctly supported.
Stabilisers or outriggers must be installed where required by the instructions.
Platforms require complete components, guardrails, toe boards, bracing and safe internal access.
Towers must be inspected after assembly and at suitable intervals, including seven-day construction inspections where applicable.
A tower must not be used in strong winds, with missing or incompatible parts, or as a support for ladders.
Before movement the height should be reduced, overhead and ground hazards checked, and all people and materials removed.
families.g: Tower-scaffold risk depends on configuration, component compatibility, base, height, outriggers, loading, wind, access, movement, inspection and user behaviour.

families.s: HSE mobile-elevating-work-platform selection and operation guidance
families.t: entrapment, overturning, falls, collision, ground, outriggers, guardrails, rescue, weather, competence and examination
f: MEWP selection and use must be planned and managed for the job and site conditions.
Major MEWP hazards include entrapment, overturning, falls and collision.
Ground must be firm and level and covers, trenches, manholes and uncompacted areas assessed for applied loads.
Outriggers should be extended and supported as required by the manufacturer's instructions.
The platform must have effective guardrails and toe boards, and falling-object risks below must be controlled.
A practised rescue plan is required and a person on the ground should know how to use the ground controls.
Operators need recognised category training plus familiarisation with the specific make and model.
MEWPs require daily checks, maintenance and thorough examination at least every six months or under a competent-person scheme.
families.g: MEWP risk depends on machine type, ground bearing capacity, outreach, loading, overhead structures, wind, traffic, rescue, operator competence, maintenance and examination.
